1:
The opening phrase has no parallel anywhere, and the voices spend more on it than on anything else. Ellicott says its meaning is largely conjectural and lists six proposals without choosing: sabbaths reckoned from the second month, the second day of Passover, the second year of the sabbatic cycle, the ecclesiastical new year, Pentecost week, or a day promoted to the honours of a first when watchmen failed to report the new moon. He prefers the last because it would explain how Luke came by so peculiar a term, and treats the phrase as a mark of the writer's wish for accuracy. Clarke concludes with Lightfoot that the day was the first sabbath after the second day of unleavened bread, adding that the disciples could not have done this before Passover without breaking two laws instead of one, since no Jew might eat green ears until then, nor after Pentecost, when the harvest was in. Barnes follows Scaliger to the same result, Calvin makes it the second of the great annual sabbaths, and Gill canvasses four theories before preferring much the same.

Two voices cut the knot. Robertson calls the reading undoubtedly spurious and reconstructs its rise: one scribe wrote first in the margin because of the sabbath miracle further down, another wrote second recalling an earlier sabbath, and a third combined them into a word found nowhere else; if it were genuine, he adds, we should not know what it means. Clarke had already reported the evidence, that the word is missing from several manuscripts and versions and that a Syriac margin notes it is not in all copies, and thinks it was dropped because the meaning was hard to fix. Henry declines the enquiry in a sentence: blessed be God we need not be critical in this matter.

On the offence the sources are unanimous and slightly amused. Robertson passes on the observation that by rabbinic reckoning rubbing the ears counted as reaping, threshing, winnowing and preparing food at once, and remarks that these Pharisees strained out gnats and swallowed camels. Barnes gathers reports from travellers who watched muleteers pluck and rub ears in passing, told it was an old custom nobody would speak against, and concludes the objection was never to the act but to the day. Cyril of Alexandria puts the retort in the second person: does not the objector himself break bread when he sets out his own sabbath meal, why blame others?

The reply from David and the shewbread is handled briefly. Henry draws the principle that ceremonial appointments may be dispensed with in cases of necessity, and that if God's own appointments could be set aside for a greater good, much more the traditions of men. On the closing claim Theophylact makes Christ speak as legislator: he is Lord of the sabbath as the one who ordained it, and so has power to loose it. Tertullian argues the same point against Marcion from the other direction: the astonishment arose because men thought it improper for Christ to proclaim the Creator as God and yet impugn his sabbath, whereas in interfering with it he acted after the Creator's own example, since the ark was carried round Jericho for eight days running and so on a sabbath.

One curiosity is preserved by two voices. Clarke and Robertson both report that an old manuscript inserts here a saying found nowhere else, addressed to a man working on the sabbath: if you know what you are doing, blessed are you, but if you do not know, you are cursed and a transgressor of the law. Clarke reads it as blessing the man who works from conviction that the old sabbath is abolished and cursing him who works from contempt, and notes the semi-barbaric word the old Latin uses for transgressor; Robertson adds that the same manuscript moves the verse about the Son of man further down.
6:
The trap is described as a dilemma. Bede sets it out: having failed against the disciples they now watch the Master, so that if he did not heal they might accuse him of cruelty or impotence, and if he did, of violating the sabbath. Clarke sharpens the verb, noting that the word for watching carries malice, and Robertson agrees the preposition adds a touch of watching on the side, assiduously like a physician at a bedside or insidiously as here. Robertson observes that the rabbis allowed saving life on the sabbath but only a Jew's, so the question cut to the quick, and that that day the watchers were plotting to destroy him.

A discrepancy between the Gospels is handled twice and differently. Augustine notes that one account has the Pharisees putting the question to the Lord while this one has him putting it to them, and reconciles them in sequence: they asked first, and he, perceiving they wanted a charge, set the man in the midst and asked in turn. Calvin allows both to stand without a sequence, since they may have spoken plainly and Christ still have discerned the design behind the words; Luke then means only that Christ saw through an intent the words did not express. Ellicott observes that this narrative and Mark's agree far more closely with each other than either does with Matthew.

Two details are claimed for the writer's profession. Robertson points out that only Luke specifies which hand was withered, calling it the physician's eye for particulars, and wonders whether he alone notes the day because as a physician he had met the same problem in practice. On the cure he observes that all three accounts use the same double compound verb, which in ordinary Greek means restoration to a former state.

Clarke uses the verse to prosecute a running quarrel with a rationalising critic. At the first mention of the hand he dismisses the claim that the word means a dislocated arm restored by the stretching without a miracle, saying it deserves no serious refutation; four verses later he grants the premise and answers it, that even had the joint slipped back, several weeks would have been needed to bring the muscles and ligaments back to tone. He closes: why all this learned labour to leave God out. He notes too that many manuscripts omit the word rendered whole, and one editor drops it.

On the fury that follows the accounts converge. Barnes lists four causes, that Christ had shown power to work a miracle, had done it against what they thought right, had thereby shown himself from God and them wrong about the sabbath, and had paid no respect to their views of the law, so that pride, obstinacy, malice and disappointed self-confidence combined; men, he adds, are often enraged when others do good in a way they do not approve. Clarke quotes to the same effect that when men have framed their conscience according to their passions, madness passes for zeal and the blackest conspiracies for pious designs. Robertson glosses the noun as lack of sense, a rage close to insanity. Ellicott raises a curiosity: Luke, who elsewhere shows so many points of contact with people connected with the Herods, omits Mark's statement that the counsel was taken with the Herodians, and suggests the very acquaintance may have made him reluctant to give them prominence. Henry draws the moral, that Christ was neither ashamed nor afraid to own the purposes of his grace though he knew his enemies would take advantage of it. Cyril of Alexandria supplies the motive on the other side, that an envious man makes the praises of others food for his own disease, and asks why Christ set the man in the midst, suggesting it may have been to move the unpitying to compassion, the malady shaming them into allaying the flames of envy.
12:
The phrase rendered in prayer to God is unique in the New Testament and splits the sources. Ellicott points out that the noun had come to mean the place set apart for prayer, the oratory by a riverside where running water allowed ablutions, and gathers instances: one apparently at Philippi, another at Halicarnassus, others at Rome attested by a satirist, one near Tiberias recorded by Josephus. On that reading the night was spent in the oratory of God. Robertson denies it flatly, allowing that sense elsewhere but insisting the word here means the actual prayer of Jesus to the Father all night long, since he needed guidance for the morning's choice; the verb for passing the whole night occurs only here, and medical writers used it of night vigils. Henry weighs the same suggestion and decides against it: Christ went into a mountain for privacy and would probably not resort to a place others frequented. Lightfoot comes at the words from the rabbinic side, quoting the tradition that God himself prays, not by supplication but by authority, confessing he cannot but laugh at their triflings, and declining to say whether the phrase should be read so.

The night itself is what the sources agree Luke wants noticed. Robertson observes that only this Gospel adds the purpose of the withdrawal, as it so often notes his habit of prayer. Henry makes it an example of secret prayer, remarking that we think half an hour a great deal to spend in the closet while Christ continued a whole night, and that after such a night one would have expected rest, whereas as soon as anyone was stirring he called his disciples. Cyril draws the same lesson, that we are taught to go apart in secret with worldly cares laid aside, the mind raised to divine contemplation.

On the choosing, Robertson stresses the middle voice, a picking out for himself from a larger body of learners, and insists Jesus took full responsibility even for the choice of Judas, who was not forced on him by the rest. Clarke lists three things that unite in a genuine apostle: he has been brought to the knowledge of God himself, has received his commission from the Head of the Church, and has his preaching accompanied by the Spirit. Ambrose finds the significance in who was passed over: not the wise, the rich or the noble, but fishermen and publicans, so no one could say men were won by riches or rank, and so the force of truth rather than the graces of oratory might prevail.

Two small difficulties are settled without fuss. Augustine notes the Judas named here appears elsewhere as Thaddeus and asks what prevents a man having two or three names; Henry adds that the order of the twelve differs in each of the three lists, teaching ministers and Christians alike not to be nice about precedence. Ellicott raises the larger problem that this Gospel places the choosing where Mark does and not where Matthew does, admits a precisely harmonised arrangement seems impossible, and calls the difficulty happily unimportant, since one or more may arrange facts otherwise than in sequence. What this record makes prominent, he adds, is that the choice came out of the night of prayer.

Augustine presses the hardest name on the list. Judas was chosen not unwittingly but knowingly, since Christ had taken human weakness upon himself and refused not even this share of human infirmity; he was willing to be betrayed by his own apostle so that a man betrayed by his friend might bear calmly his mistaken judgment and his kindness thrown away. Henry calls the twelve happy as the queen of Sheba called the servants of Solomon happy, and observes that one of them had a devil and proved a traitor, yet Christ in choosing him was not deceived.
17:
Whether the discourse that follows is the Sermon on the Mount occupies most of the comment, the answers differing in confidence rather than substance. Barnes gives three reasons for identity, that they begin and close alike, their substance is the same, and in both the centurion's servant is healed next; against these he weighs the objections that one has a mountain and the other a plain, one Christ sitting where the other has him standing. He resolves it by observing that this Gospel never says the sermon was delivered on the plain, only that the healing was, so Christ may have withdrawn again to an eminence and sat down to speak. Clarke agrees and calls the whole picture striking: the ascent, the night of prayer, the authoritative separating of the twelve from the mass, the descent, the healing of the diseased in the plain. Robertson is blunter: there is not the slightest reason for making one evangelist put the sermon on the mountain and the other in the valley, since the level place may lie on the mountain side, where he stopped his descent and found a slight elevation to speak from.

Ellicott is least willing to settle it. He grants the resemblances are so many that identity has often been supposed, and offers a partial explanation: this Gospel and Mark distinguish the choice of the twelve from their later mission, which meets us further on in a form implying the twelve already existed as a body. The difficulty is not dissolved: events these two place even before the choice are placed by Matthew after the mission. On the phrase itself he corrects the article, since the Greek has none and the sense is on a plain or level place, and observes that the description of the crowd resembles both Mark's and Matthew's before the Sermon on the Mount.

Robertson also defends the reports against another charge. It is quite gratuitous, he says, to argue that the evangelists made up this sermon out of isolated sayings, since both give too much local detail of place and audience; he allows that Jesus repeated many of these sayings elsewhere, and lays the greater length of the other report to its argument about the rabbis' righteousness.

The composition of the crowd is what the eastern voices seize on. Cyril of Alexandria stresses that the election was not made in a corner but before a vast concourse from all Judea and the sea coast, those coastal hearers being idolaters, partly observing Jewish customs yet not wholly abandoning their idols; teachers were appointed in sight of all, for everyone beneath heaven, and the apostles afterwards summoned Jews from a merely legal worship and Greeks from the service of demons. Ambrose finds the antithesis in the movement: Christ ascends with his apostles and descends to the multitude, since the crowd could not see him except in a lowly place, and neither follows him to the heights nor climbs them; when he descends he finds the sick, for in high places there are none.

On the virtue that went out of him the comment is warm. Robertson reads the imperfects as a picture of a surging crowd pressing up, thinks some probably felt a kind of virtue or magic in the garments, and renders the clauses as continuous, power was coming out from him and he kept on healing all; he cannot leave it without the application that a preacher who is no vehicle of power from Christ may well ask himself why. He notes too that two different verbs for healing stand side by side, one the term more usual for professional cures, with no distinction drawn. Cyril turns the phrase into an argument about the healer: Christ did not borrow strength from another, but being God by nature, though he had become flesh, healed them all by the putting forth of his own power.
20:
The missing words are the first question. This report has blessed are the poor where the other has poor in spirit, and Ellicott makes the omission decisive: if the two discourses were one, this evangelist or his informant dropped singularly important words that had actually been spoken, a far greater difficulty than supposing that Christ varied the aspects of a truth he presented more than once. He therefore treats them as spoken on different occasions. Cyril of Alexandria harmonises differently: the evangelists do not contradict but divide the narrative between them and often recapitulate. Cyril distinguishes the senses: with the addition it means a modest and depressed mind, without it those who despise riches, as suited men about to preach the gospel. Basil cautions that not everyone oppressed by poverty is blessed, but he who has preferred the commandment of Christ to worldly riches; many are poor in possessions and most covetous in disposition, whom poverty does not save but their affections condemn. Nothing involuntary deserves a blessing, because all virtue is characterised by freedom of the will.

Ellicott makes two smaller corrections. The English blessed be leaves it unclear whether a fact is declared or a prayer offered, and should be blessed are; the kingdom named is of God, not of heaven. It seems to have been this writer's particular aim, he adds, to gather the teaching on the danger of riches. Robertson notices the lifted eyes peculiar to the opening, the audience looked full in the face, and cannot resist adding that some preachers neither open their mouths nor look up.

On mourning Chrysostom writes the fullest note. Godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, and Paul, having no failings of his own, mourned for those of others; such grief is the source of gladness, and a man who weeps for others' sins will not leave his own unwept nor fall easily into sin. He ends: we often find the Lord sorrowing, never laughing.

The woes are the distinguishing feature of this report. Calvin finds the correspondence exact, four blessings answered by four curses, the contrast meant to strike terror into the ungodly and to rouse believers, who are prone to be intoxicated by prosperity and to envy the reprobate. He restricts the curse: it falls not on all the rich but on those so occupied with possessions that they forget the life to come, since riches are so far from making a man happy that they often become the means of his ruin; and poor Lazarus was received into the bosom of rich Abraham. Ellicott hears pity rather than denunciation and would render it woe for you, reading the consolation already received as meaning they have all they understand or care for, and therefore all they can have, the verb being that used of those who have their reward.

Barnes fills in the psychology. The rich had loved wealth, sought it and found their consolation in it, and would not seek it from the gospel, being too proud to ask, too satisfied to want it, too full of cares to attend to it; the fulness meant is that of men satisfied with what supplies the body and anxious for no enduring riches. Ellicott sharpens the same word into the satiety of over-indulgence, and hears in laughter turned to mourning an echo of the epistle of James.

Tertullian uses the woe differently. Against Marcion he argues that a Christ come to destroy the prophets could not consistently stigmatise their persecutors, so their defence belongs to the Creator's Christ, who fulfilled their predictions; and presses the pronouncement itself as evidence, since a god who condescends to curse proves himself capable of anger, and no longer the impassible deity his opponents describe. Whether the word carries the force of a curse or only an admonition he calls immaterial, since an admonition is never given without the sting of a threat.
27:
The address is the first question. Henry takes it widely, to all that hear and not to disciples only, these being lessons of universal concern; Wesley reads a change of audience, our Lord having spoken hitherto to particular sorts and now to all in general. Gill dissents: the hearers meant are those who have received the traditions of the elders, which the rules that follow oppose. Robertson puts the weight on the contrastive particle, the only one of the antitheses set out at length in the other report that this evangelist keeps; love of enemies is in the Old Testament, he grants, but Jesus ennobles the verb by using it of them. Bede marks the hinge: having spoken of what they might suffer from their enemies, he now shows how they ought to behave towards them.

Chrysostom supplies the governing image. Physicians attacked by madmen have then most compassion on them; have the like consideration towards your persecutors, who are under the greatest infirmity, and do not cease until they have exhausted all their bitterness. On the closing rule he observes that it is put positively, since there are two ways to virtue, abstaining from evil and doing good, and naming one signifies the other; the command lies within nature, Christ having ordained nothing surpassing it but what he had long before implanted in our conscience, so that your own will is the law to you. Basil turns it on the powerful, who account as enemies all who treat them with less consideration than they think they deserve; it is a great dishonour in a prince to be ready to take revenge, for how shall he teach another to return no evil for evil if he retaliates.

The garments are handled philologically. Clarke, following Bishop Pearce, distinguishes the under garment from the outer, citing Horace, Maximus Tyrius and Plutarch. Ellicott observes that this report inverts the order, the upper garment taken and the under one offered, and that where the other points to legal process this points to violence. Robertson agrees the blow is violence rather than contempt, and adds the difficulty honestly: sticklers for extreme literalism find trouble with Jesus protesting when he received a slap. He renders the prohibition do not hinder him in his robbing, and remarks that it is usually useless anyhow with modern armed bandits. Wesley treats both clauses as proverbial for an invasion of the tenderest points of honour and property. Cyril reads it as a schooling in contempt of property, the soul's virtue being alien from the pleasure of wealth, the merciful man conferring on persecutors the benefits by which he assists his friends.

On asking nothing back the voices divide. Calvin denies the clause concerns a request for assistance: it speaks of actions at law which bad men raise to carry off the property of others, expounding the patient bearing of the spoiling of our goods. He guards it at once: we ought not to quibble about words as if a good man might not recover his own when God gives him the lawful means; we are enjoined only to wait, undistressed, till the Lord calls the robbers to account. Clarke reads it of extortion instead, the way tax-gatherers and soldiers spoiled the people, warning against begging the goods off lest more be seized; he quotes Virgil on the harpies and the son of Sirach on the man who to-day lendeth and to-morrow asks it again. Robertson finds the force in the tense, a prohibition of the habit of asking back. Henry, following Hammond, takes the goods as borrowed rather than stolen, and would not have providence's insolvents taken by the throat.

Henry states the golden rule as putting our souls into their souls' stead. Ellicott ends with a harmonising argument: the very different arrangement of the precepts in the two discourses is obviously an argument against their identity.
32:
The comparison with sinners is read two ways. Clarke takes the word for heathens, where the other report has tax-gatherers, and warns that a man should tremble who finds in his life nothing beyond what a Turk's life shows. Ellicott sees rather the writer's Gentile audience, the wider term replacing the one that pointed the maxim for Jews, ; what thank have ye looks to expected gratitude, what reward have ye to concrete payment. Wesley presses the sting: our Lord has so little regard for the returning of love for love, the highest instance of natural virtue, that he does not account it to deserve thanks; a man may do it who has not taken a step in Christianity. Chrysostom explains why: nothing earthly engenders spiritual love, neither gain nor kindness nor nature nor time, and it is not even overcome of malice; Paul went to those who stoned him to do them good, and Moses, stoned by the Jews, prayed for them.

The clause about lending is where the sources part company. Gregory of Nyssa calls the harsh calculation of interest theft or homicide without fear of erring: what difference is there between digging under a wall and possessing property by a compulsory rate? Basil elaborates the figure the Greek name suggests: animals cease breeding once they transfer their bringing forth to their young, but interest brings forth as soon as it is born, and the money of the covetous both increases and renews the capital. Touch not the destructive monster; asked how one is to live, he answers work, serve, last of all beg, anything being more tolerable than borrowing upon interest. He turns the precept into security: giving to a poor man is gift and loan at once, no return being hoped for yet God restoring it; will you accept a rich citizen as surety and reject God surety for the poor? Tertullian reads the older prohibitions as graduated preparation, the law first eradicating the fruit of the money lent, to accustom a man to losing the money itself.

Calvin denies the application altogether. It is a mistake to confine the statement to usury, as if Christ forbade only usurers, the preceding verses having a wider reference; he exhorts us to perform our duties freely, mercenary acts being of no account with God; kindness done in hope of reward is not condemned, but carries no weight as a testimony of charity. The dispute turns on a word. Ellicott prefers in nothing losing hope, since the verb uniformly means to despair in the version this writer knew, and notes a variant pronoun giving driving no man to despair; Clarke reports the same variant from Bishop Pearce, as not cutting off any man's hope. Robertson blames a translation: the received meaning has no parallel anywhere, and the Latin hoping for nothing thence has wrought great havoc in Europe, since on its strength popes and councils repeatedly condemned the taking of any interest, so that money-lending passed to the Jews and added greatly to the detestation in which they were held. What is forbidden, he holds, is despairing of repayment: we are to help the apparently hopeless cases, as medical writers use the word.

On the conclusion the voices converge. Clarke calls the command to love enemies the most sublime precept ever delivered to man, one a false religion durst not give. Ellicott notes that sons of the Most High is the only place where our Lord applies this name to the Father, and that merciful stands where the other has perfect, the noblest of the divine attributes; he sends the reader to Shakespeare on the quality of mercy. Robertson adds that in both, the perfection of the Father is the goal, and in neither is it said the children have reached it. Cyril closes: mercy makes us like to God, imprinting on our souls signs of a heavenly nature.
37:
The three prohibitions read as a descent. Ellicott finds something like a climax, seek not to judge at all, and if you must judge be not eager to condemn; he corrects the last verb to set free or acquit, a quasi-judicial act rather than the forgiveness of a private wrong. Robertson makes the point grammatically, the present imperative forbidding the habit of criticism, not the forming of opinions but the forming of them rashly; release is the positive command opposite to the censoriousness condemned. Cyril traces the fault to its root: men look into the things of others and forget their own passions.

The measure draws out the antiquarians. Lightfoot produces the temple's two tithing measures, one heaped and one struck level, all heaped save the high priest's, since flour divided into two tenths would spill; the rabbis asked whether the filling of the priest's hand was struck or heaped, and answered neither, but floating over. Ellicott and Barnes explain the bosom as the large fold of an Eastern dress used as a pocket. Clarke illustrates it from Herodotus, where Alcmaeon, promised as much of Croesus's gold as he could carry at once, wore the widest tunic and largest buskins he could find and loaded even his hair with ingots. He notes too that the closing maxim stands in the Jerusalem Targum, a rule his hearers already allowed.

Whether the promise holds is disputed. Henry states it flatly: those merciful to other people's names shall find others merciful to theirs, and those who deal hardly must own with Adoni-bezek that God is righteous when paid in their own coin; yet providence does not always go by this rule, the exact retributions being reserved for another world. Calvin presses harder. The children of God frequently receive the very worst reward and are oppressed by unjust slanders even when they have spared the faults of brethren; promises relating to the present life do not always hold, and God permits the innocent to be overwhelmed that he may humble them and at length maintain the goodness of their cause. He adds a second cause: believers are themselves carried away by excessive severity and by their own fault provoke a similar judgment, since no man is as kind to his brethren as he ought to be. Theophylact meets the arithmetical objection, that if the return runs over it cannot be the same measure, : the promise says the same measure, not just as great a one, and the running over is that mercy is shown a thousand times.

Ellicott calls the parable a break with no parallel in the other sermon, and an instance of the wider sense of the word, any proverbial saying involving a similitude; Robertson reports Plummer's view that the second half of the sermon begins here; and Gill and Calvin both hold the sayings were gathered rather than spoken at one time.

The saying about the disciple is applied three ways. Barnes takes it of attainment: followers do not go beyond their teachers, and blind guides breed blind followers. Ellicott admits the connection of thought is obscure and some links may have been omitted, then supplies one: the Master taught but did not judge, and were they above him that they should do what he refrained from doing? Cyril reaches the same end more shortly: since Christ judged not, why judge you, for he came not to judge the world but to show mercy. On the participle Clarke follows the medical writers who use the verb of reducing a dislocated limb, and takes it of thorough instruction; Calvin declines both Erasmus and the old translator because Christ speaks not of perfection but of resemblance; Robertson keeps the mending sense and says it is a long process to get the pupil patched up to the plane of his teacher. Robertson hears the sting in the change from brother to hypocrite.
43:
The tree continues the rebuke. Bede reads it against the hypocrites: what you set forth in words make up also in works, for the hypocrite who does evil works is not good though he pretends, and the innocent who does good works is not evil though blamed. Isidore of Pelusium guards the figure from fatalism: what is excluded is not repentance but continuance in evil, which bears no good fruit while it lasts and yields abundantly once converted; what nature is to the tree, our affections are to us, and if a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit, how shall a corrupt heart? Chrysostom states the logic: the fruit is caused by the tree, yet the fruit is what brings us knowledge of the tree. In the other report, Gill observes, the saying is aimed at false teachers; here it falls on men busy censuring their brethren.

Ellicott notes that the pairing differs, thorns going with grapes and figs with thistles in the other report, and that the word for bramble is the Greek Old Testament's word for the burning bush. Robertson confirms it, and passes on the remark that Galen has a chapter on the bramble's medicinal uses. Ambrose allegorises: the grape nearest the ground is rotten and ripens on the higher branches, so none escapes the condemnation of the flesh but he whom Christ redeemed, who hung on the tree as a grape.

On the treasure of the heart, the question is what is judged. Cyril sees the same thing under another figure. Ellicott recalls that in the other report the words follow the charge about casting out devils, and reads the good treasure as yielding kindness and compassion where the hypocrite, judging others by himself, yields bitterness and uncharitable condemnation. Calvin narrows it to doctrine: believers must examine what is taught by those professing to serve God, titles being of little value till the speaker gives evidence that he is sent. He raises the objection that tongues lie and the worst hearts are often the best speakers, answering that Christ points out only what ordinarily happens, so the tongue may still be called the index of the mind. Robertson quotes Plummer: when men are natural, heart and mouth act in concert, but otherwise the mouth sometimes professes what the heart does not feel.

On the title Bede asks why they boast of the leaves of a right confession and show no fruit of good works; Clarke has the tongue for a pump which empties the heart but neither fills nor cleanses it, the love of God being the hidden spring; Robertson says simply that this is the point about every sermon that counts.

The building is where the detail lies. Robertson makes the digging the whole point, two plain aorists, no Hebraism, the wise builder striking rock before he laid the foundation; the word for flood occurs only here, and the word for the ruin is used in medicine of a laceration. Ellicott finds this report less full, the other adding rain and wind, but stronger at the end: the flood had no power to shake the house where the other only says it fell not; and the better copies give because it had been well built, the received reading altered later to agree with the other. Clarke closes with a warning from a rigid predestinarian: neither by the speculations of astrologers nor by the Calvinian assurance of predestination do we discover our portion, but by examination of the heart and of the life. Augustine uses the shared ending to argue harmony: the two discourses open alike and end altogether the same, and the difference of mountain and plain is met by supposing our Lord first on a higher part of the mountain with his disciples alone, then descending to level ground on the mountain side, standing till the crowds gathered and afterwards sitting to speak.
